Q: How do I add execute permission to a file in CVS after it's already been checked in? A:

Per http://cvsbook.red-bean.com/cvsbook.html - CVS keeps changing file permissions; why does it do that?:

In general, CVS doesn't do a very good job of preserving permissions on files. When you import a project and then check it out, there is no guarantee that the file permissions in the new working copy will be the same as when the project was imported. More likely, the working copy files will be created with the same standard permissions that you normally get on newly created files.

However, there is at least one exception. If you want to store executable shell scripts in the project, you can keep them executable in all working copies by making the corresponding repository file executable:

floss$ ls -l /usr/local/newrepos/someproj
total 6
-r--r--r--   1 jrandom  users         630 Aug 17 01:10 README.txt,v
-r-xr-xr-x   1 jrandom  users        1041 Aug 17 01:10 scrub.pl,v* <-------
-r--r--r--   1 jrandom  users         750 Aug 17 01:10 hello.c,v

Notice that although the file is executable, it is still read-only, as all repository files should be (remember that CVS works by making a temporary copy of the RCS file, doing everything in the copy, and then replacing the original with the copy when ready).

When you import or add an executable file, CVS preserves the executable bits, so if the permissions were correct from the start, you have nothing to worry about. However, if you accidentally add the file before making it executable, you must go into the repository and manually set the RCS file to be executable.

The repository permissions always dominate. If the file is nonexecutable in the repository, but executable in the working copy, the working copy file will also be nonexecutable after you do an update.

Q: Multiple groups based on conditions in SQL A: 
Hello as already suggested you can replace the subquery moving the conditions in the Qualify clause in this way:


select t.*, 
min( colc)over(partition by cola, colb)  as min_index,
max( colc)over(partition by cola, colb) as max_index, 
sum(case when cold='R004' then 1 else 0 end) over (partition by cola, colb, colc) as R004Flag
from yourtable t
qualify (max_index <> min_index AND  R004Flag =0) OR (max_index = min_index AND  (R004Flag =1 or R004Flag =0));

And this is one way you can solve the issue with count distinct in teradata using dense_rank function which is supported:

select t.*,  
dense_rank() over (partition by cola, colb order by colc)   
+ dense_rank() over (partition by cola, colb  order by colc desc)-1  as cntd,
 sum(case when cold='R004' then 1 else 0 end)
         over ( partition by cola, colb, colc) as R004Flag
from yourtable t
qualify (cntd>1 AND  R004Flag =0) OR (cntd=1 AND  (R004Flag =1 or R004Flag =0));

Hope it helps.

Q: Lifetime of temporary to which a local reference is bound in a c++ coroutine A:

As you quoted from cpprefernce:

Each coroutine is associated with

...

  • the coroutine state, which is internal, dynamically-allocated storage (unless the allocation is optimized out), object that contains

...

  • local variables and temporaries whose lifetime spans the current suspension point.

(emphasis is mine)

In the "normal" (non-coroutine) case the following code:

const auto& ref = std::string("abc");

Will extend the life of the temporary because of the bounding to the const-ref. This seems like exactly the case mentioned above (with my emphasis in bold).

Therefore there is no dangling reference in your code:
The std::string temporary object will be kept as a part of the coroutine state and the reference will alias it.

Q: ADK Google Gemini: "Session not found: default when" using InMemoryRunner with LlmAgent A:

InMemoryRunner creates its own InMemorySessionService() instance. When you create sessions in a global _SESSION_SERVICE, the runner can't find them because it's looking in its own separate service instance.

_APP_USER_ID = "system"
_APP_SESSION_ID = "default"
# Global services to persist state across calls
_SESSION_SERVICE = InMemorySessionService()


async def _run_agent(agent: Agent, prompt: str) -> str:
    session = await _SESSION_SERVICE.create_session(
        app_name="duck_pa",
        user_id=_APP_USER_ID,
        session_id=_APP_SESSION_ID
    )

    runner = InMemoryRunner(agent, app_name=session.app_name)
    # Patch the runner with our global session service
    runner.session_service = _SESSION_SERVICE
    #...

You also need to decide whether to make the artifact and memory service global considering your approach.

In that case that all these services are global, constructing the runner using InMemoryRunner is no longer necessary.

from google.adk.apps.app import App
from google.adk.runners import Runner

_APP_USER_ID = "system"
_APP_SESSION_ID = "default"
# Global services to persist state across calls
_SESSION_SERVICE = InMemorySessionService()
_ARTIFACT_SERVICE = InMemoryArtifactService()
_MEMORY_SERVICE = InMemoryMemoryService()

async def _run_agent(agent: Agent, prompt: str) -> str:
    session = await _SESSION_SERVICE.create_session(
        app_name="duck_pa",
        user_id=_APP_USER_ID,
        session_id=_APP_SESSION_ID
    )

    # Use the App pattern (recommended by ADK maintainers)
    app = App(
        name="duck_pa",
        root_agent=agent
    )

    runner = Runner(
        app=app,  # Recommended: use App instead of separate agent/app_name
        session_service=_SESSION_SERVICE,
        artifact_service=_ARTIFACT_SERVICE,
        memory_service=_MEMORY_SERVICE,
    )
    #...

Q: Run Ansible playbook without inventory A:

Besides using a minimal inventory file that defines localhost explicitly, you can alternatively rely on the implicit localhost, ansible will provide, like this:

$ ansible-playbook -i /dev/null someplaybook.yml

However, then you likely need to change your hosts: declaration in your playbook to:

- name: some playbook
  hosts: localhost

  roles:
      - somerole

Since the implicit localhost doesn't match all nor groups.

NB: The above ansible-playbook command uses -i /dev/null such that it doesn't fall back to reading the default $HOME/hosts inventory file locations.
